newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Drought forces decline in Tanzanian cotton crop.
newsitem.headline: Drought forces decline in Tanzanian cotton crop.

text.p: Severe drought in Tanzanias main cotton growing areas will cause a sharp drop in cotton production in 1996/97 (October-September), a senior industry official said on Sunday.
Ali Ngongolo told Reuters in an interview that low rainfall in late 1996 around Lake Victoria meant production would reach about 350,000 bales in 1996/97 from 430,000 bales in 1995/96.

Ngongolo, general manager of the Tanzania Cotton Lint and Seed Board, said earnings in 1996/97 were forecast to drop to $83 million from $109 million in 1995/96 and $115 million in 1994/95. Production in 1994/95 was 440,000 bales.
One bale is the equivalent of 181 kg (399.105 lbs).
"The reason why we project a decline is poor weather," Ngongolo told Reuters. "Most of the main growing areas around Lake Victoria did not get adequate rains to support planting."
"Cotton in Tanzania depends on weather. We do not irrigate our crop. It is rain-fed."
The lowest production was around 200,000 bales in 1974/75.

Farms also face an aphid attack that could further undermine quality and production. "Because of the drought, we could encounter problems with aphids. They suck water out of the plant and make it weaker," Ngongolo said.
Tanzania accounts for less than one percent of world production dominated by Australia, Russia, China and the United States.
Tanzanias cotton is highly regarded due to quality. It is classified as a medium staple and is hand-picked, a measure that further ensures high quality.
Ngongolo said that in the 1995/96 season the board purchased about two percent of the annual crop, with the rest bought by private buyers following reforms in the industry.
Union-run cotton cooperatives account for 30 ginneries while private ginneries total 15. Some two million Tanzanian families or 10 million people derive a living from cotton production.
Their mostly peasant holdings average in size between 0.5 and 3.0 hectares (1.23 and 7.413 acres). Land under cotton is estimated at up to 400,000 hectares (988,400 acres).
Domestic use of cotton is about 30,000 bales, down from a peak of 100,000 bales in the 1980s, according to Ngongolo.
Textile production in Tanzania has declined dramatically with most state-owned mills heavily in debt and up for sale in the government's privatisation drive.
Tanzania's main cotton export markets are Europe, Taiwan and Malaysia.

Increased investment in the sector could ensure its future viability and was actively encouraged by the government, said Ngongolo, adding that a combination of good weather and higher investment could result in annual production of up to one million bales that would make cotton a top export performer.
